Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

NEW YORK (CNN) -- Five new cases of the H1N1 virus in New York City schools will force three schools to close for a week, Mayor Michael Bloomberg said at a news conference Thursday evening. The city is temporarily closing the schools to "slow transmission" of the virus, Mayor Michael Bloomberg said. The two intermediate schools and one primary school are in Queens, and all three will be closed for at least five days, the mayor said. "We are closing the schools to slow transmission" of sickness, he said. Bloomberg, flanked by New York Gov. David Paterson and New York City School Chancellor Joel Klein, said four students at one of the intermediate schools have the virus and an administrator was critically ill Thursday with H1N1. Bloomberg indicated the school administrator had a pre-existing medical condition. Fifty students at that school have been sent home with flu-like symptoms since May 6. At the two other schools, the primary school had an overflowing nurse's office Thursday, reporting 29 students suffering from flu-like symptoms. The other intermediate school had 241 students absent with illness Thursday. The New York City Department of Health and the Department of Education have been in nearly constant contact, said Jason Post, a spokesman from Bloomberg's office. When there's a spike in students absent from classes, the Department of Health is alerted. "There's always good communication, flu or no flu," Post said. "But our senses have been sharp for a while now." The Health Department has seen a general increase in flu activity in Queens, officials said in a news release. While the symptoms of H1N1 flu seem to resemble those of seasonal flu, the H1N1 virus appears to spread more extensively, at least in schools, warranting closures to slow transmission in the community, the release said. Dr. Isaac Weisfuse, the deputy commissioner of the city's Department of Hygiene and Mental Health, said although concern is legitimate, there's no solid evidence that suggests the H1N1 flu -- also known as swine flu -- is more dangerous than the flu in general. "The bottom line is if you're sick, stay home," Weisfuse said. "And don't go back to school until you're better for one whole day." In late April, St. Francis Prep, a high school in Queens, was closed because of a flu outbreak. Since then, the school reopened and the stricken students have recovered, according to the mayor's office. "As we have said from the outset of the appearance of H1N1 in our city last month, we will share with New Yorkers what we know and not speculate on what we don't know," said Bloomberg in a statement. According to the World Health Organization and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, as of Thursday night 7,412 cases of H1N1 flu have been confirmed worldwide. The organizations said 63 deaths attributed to the virus have been confirmed worldwide. The CDC said 4,298 cases of the virus and three fatalities have been confirmed in the United States as of Thursday night. New York had 224 confirmed cases of H1N1, the CDC said. It was not clear whether the five cases cited by Bloomberg and the other New York officials were included in the latest CDC total.

**NEW YORK** -- New York City health officials ordered the closure of three Queens schools for a week Thursday after five new cases of H1N1 swine flu were confirmed among students, city officials announced.

The decision affects hundreds of students and comes as health authorities work to contain the spread of the virus that has now reached multiple continents.

"We are taking these precautions out of an abundance of caution to protect our children and our communities," Mayor Michael Bloomberg said at a news conference. "The health and safety of our students is our top priority, and we will not hesitate to take necessary action based on the guidance of our health experts."

The five confirmed cases prompted swift action from the city's Department of Health and Mental Hygiene, which recommended the temporary closures to prevent further transmission among the student population.

"When we see clusters of cases in a school setting, closing the facility temporarily is one of the most effective tools we have to slow the spread," said a Health Department spokesperson. "We are monitoring the situation closely and will reassess before the schools reopen."

## Precautionary Measures

Health officials emphasized that the closures are precautionary and that most cases of the H1N1 virus have been mild. Students and parents were advised to watch for flu-like symptoms, including fever, cough, sore throat and body aches, and to seek medical attention if symptoms develop.

City officials also urged residents to take basic preventive steps, including frequent hand-washing, covering coughs and sneezes, and staying home when sick.

"Simple measures can make a big difference," Bloomberg added. "We're asking every New Yorker to do their part."

## Case Statistics

The World Health Organization has confirmed thousands of H1N1 cases worldwide across multiple countries, as the outbreak continues to draw international concern. Health agencies around the globe have raised alert levels and stepped up surveillance efforts.

In the United States, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed hundreds of cases across numerous states, with the number continuing to climb as testing expands. Officials have cautioned that the actual number of infections is likely higher than confirmed cases suggest.

The CDC has continued to recommend that schools with confirmed cases consider closures, while advising communities to prepare for the possibility of wider spread.

## Looking Ahead

The three Queens schools are expected to remain closed for approximately one week, pending further evaluation by health authorities. Officials said they would provide updates as the situation develops.

"We will get through this together," Bloomberg said. "New Yorkers are resilient, and by staying informed and taking sensible precautions, we can keep our city healthy and safe."

**QUEENS, N.Y.** — City health and education officials ordered the closure of three Queens schools this week after a surge in flu-like illness among students and staff, as an assistant principal at one of the affected schools remained in critical condition, according to officials.

The closures affect two intermediate schools and one primary school, sidelining thousands of students as public health authorities work to slow the spread of the H1N1 virus, commonly known as swine flu.

## An Administrator Fighting for His Life

At the center of community concern is a veteran assistant principal who fell gravely ill and was hospitalized in critical condition. Officials confirmed the administrator was placed on a ventilator as physicians worked to stabilize his condition. Colleagues described him as a beloved fixture in the school community, and word of his hospitalization sent a wave of anxiety through parents and staff.

Health officials cautioned against drawing immediate conclusions about the severity of the outbreak based on a single case, noting that even seasonal influenza can produce serious complications in some individuals.

## Why the Schools Were Closed

The Department of Education and the city's Department of Health made the decision to close the schools after hundreds of students reported absences with flu-like symptoms, including fever, sore throat, cough, and body aches. Officials said the closures were a precautionary measure intended to limit transmission and allow for cleaning of the buildings.

"The health and safety of our students and staff is our top priority," a Department of Education spokesperson said. "Closing these schools temporarily gives us the opportunity to assess the situation and take appropriate steps."

The schools are expected to remain closed for several days, though officials said the timeline could change based on developing conditions.

## Public Health Guidance

Health authorities urged parents and residents to take standard precautions to reduce the spread of the virus:

- **Keep sick children home.** Students exhibiting fever or flu-like symptoms should not attend school and should remain home until at least 24 hours after their fever subsides.
- **Practice good hygiene.** Frequent handwashing with soap and water, and covering coughs and sneezes, remain among the most effective preventive measures.
- **Watch for warning signs.** Parents were advised to seek immediate medical attention if a child experiences difficulty breathing, bluish skin, persistent vomiting, or sudden dizziness.
- **Avoid emergency rooms for mild cases.** Officials asked residents with mild symptoms to contact their primary care physicians rather than overwhelming hospital emergency departments.

Health officials emphasized that the majority of H1N1 cases have been mild, with most patients recovering fully without hospitalization. Nevertheless, they urged the public to remain vigilant, particularly for individuals in higher-risk groups, including young children, pregnant women, and those with underlying medical conditions.

## A Community on Edge

For parents in the affected neighborhoods, the closures have created both anxiety and logistical challenges as they scramble to arrange childcare. Outside one shuttered school, families gathered to exchange information and voice concerns about their children's health.

"You hear about the assistant principal, and it makes it very real," said one parent. "We just want to know everyone is going to be okay."

City officials pledged to keep families informed as the situation evolves and said they would continue monitoring absentee rates and illness reports across the borough. Additional school closures have not been ruled out should the outbreak spread.

Officials said updates would be provided through the Department of Education and Department of Health, and encouraged residents to consult official channels for the latest guidance.

---

*This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.*
